background.definition: Pyloric stenosis (PS), a progressive narrowing of the pyloric canal due to hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle in infancy, is characterized by projectile emesis, palpable pyloric mass, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

list.listitem: Overall incidence of 2 to 12.3 per 1000 live births in the United States.
4:1 male to female ratio.
White: 2.4 per 1000 live births.
Hispanic: 1.8 per 1000 live births.
Black: 0.7 per 1000 live births.
Asian: 0.6 per 1000 live births.
Decreased incidence in patients of mixed ethnicity.
Incidence is higher if mothers are 20 to 24 years old (2.3/1000) compared with mothers older than 24 years (1.7/1000).
Incidence is higher in firstborn children (2.2/1000) and lower in fifthborn children (1.3/1000).
Likely multifactorial: familial and environmental.

Macrolide use in infants at age 3 to 13 days and exposure through breastmilk are associated with increased risk of pyloric stenosis. However, prenatal use of macrolides by the mother is not associated with an increased risk of pyloric stenosis.
Pyloric stenosis has been reported in patients with partial trisomy 9 involving bands q22.1-31.3.
Deficient nitric oxide synthase and decreased neurotrophin production have been noted in the pyloric muscle of patients with PS.

In a population-based cohort study of 70,148 neonates in Denmark, there was an increased risk of pyloric stenosis among bottle-fed infants compared with exclusively breastfed infants (HR: 4.6; 95% CI: 2.8-7.7).
Abnormal innervation and defective relaxation of the pyloric muscle result in pyloric muscle hypertrophy and subsequent narrowing of pyloric canal leading to gastric outlet obstruction.
Loss of H+ and Cl− from emesis induces compensatory urinary loss of Na+ and HCO3 −.
Persistent emesis leads to urinary excretion of K+ and H+.

Differential.Differential_Features: Usual onset in early newborn period
Variability of pyloric muscle thickness or length by ultrasonography
Acute onset of emesis, diarrhea, and possible fever with spontaneous resolution
Symptoms resolve when treated with appropriate formula
Symptoms resolve with appropriate quantity of feeding
Bowel malrotation with or without volvulus
Crampy pain, bloody stools, increasing lethargy
Usually in premature infants and accompanied by bloody stools

list.listitem: Consider PS in infants up to 20 weeks of age with progressive projectile nonbilious emesis. Infants are typically hungry following emesis. Weight loss can occur with prolonged emesis.
Insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression facilitates palpation of the olive or pyloric tumor in the RUQ.
Feeding the infant by mouth or by nasogastric tube helps prevent crying during the exam and also allows visualization of peristaltic waves.

Palpable olive has been noted in 74% to 87% of patients with PS and has positive predictive value of 99.3%. Presence of palpable olive is not related to duration of emesis or presence of electrolyte abnormalities.
However, a systematic review of 43 studies with 6085 infants found a wide range of sensitivity (10% to 93%) for palpation.
Diagnostic tests are not necessary if an olive is palpable.
Electrolytes might be normal, but PS can lead to hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
Of patients less than 12 weeks old who present to an emergency department with emesis and suspected PS, a combination of serum pH > 7.45, chloride < 98 mEq/L, and base excess > 3 mEq/L was helpful.

Abdominal ultrasonography is the radiologic test of choice. Ultrasound findings consistent with PS include pyloric muscle thickness of at least 3 mm (LR+ 99, LR- 0.01) or length of at least 14 mm (100% sensitive, 97% specific), or both.

A systematic review of 43 studies with 6085 infants found that pyloric muscle thickness (PMT) ≥ 3 mm on ultrasound was highly accurate (LR+ 81, LR- 0.024), as was pyloric ratio ≥ 0.26 and a channel length of at least 14 mm.
Transverse wall thickness of 3 mm is therefore the optimal cutoff for diagnosis, as is pyloric ratio (wall thickness/pyloric diameter) of 0.27 or higher.

Upper GI findings consistent with PS include the "string sign" of elongated pylorus, "beak sign" of filling of proximal pylorus, "shoulder sign" of filling of antrum, and "railroad track sign" of parallel lines in pylorus.

Upper GI and ultrasonography have similar sensitivity and specificity. However, while ultrasonography has the benefit of no radiation exposure, upper GI is useful to assess for other anatomic anomalies that cause emesis. Premature infants have shorter pyloric length compared to term infants, which is due to lower body weight in preterm infants; pyloric length increases by 1.13 mm per kilogram of body weight.
Plain film abdominal radiograph is not useful in PS diagnosis, but it might show gastric distension or impression of the hypertrophic pyloric muscle on an air-filled gastric antrum.

Pyloromyotomy can use a laparoscoic approach (LAP) or open approach. LAP is associated with a non-significantly higher risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy, but there was no difference in rates of post-operative infections or complications. A
Postoperative oral feedings ad lib shorten the time to full feeds and time to discharge.B
IV atropine sulfate at a dose of 0.04 to 0.12 mg/kg/day for 7 days was successful to treat PS in 76% of patients.
Transient side effects were tachycardia and flushed skin.
Indicated in patients for whom surgery is contraindicated.

The traditional Ramstedt pyloromyotomy consists of division along length of hypertrophied pylorus muscle through RUQ transverse incision. Surgical techniques designed to improve cosmetic outcome, including LAP, infraumbilical rim, and circumumbilical (UMB) skinfold approaches, are effective alternatives.

The laparoscopic (LAP), right upper quadrant (RUQ) transverse incision, and infraumbilical rim and circumumbilical (UMB) techniques are similar in complication rate, time to full feeds, and length of hospital stay, but LAP requires less postoperative analgesia.
An RCT found that the LAP technique leads to less postoperative emesis than RUQ technique but has a similar duration of surgery.
Another RCT found that the LAP technique has a longer duration of surgery and anesthesia than the UMB technique, but has a similar rate of postoperative emesis.

A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 720 patients randomized to LAP or open pyloromyotomy. There was a trend toward a higher risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy with LAP (RR 7.4, 95% CI 0.9 - 59) but no difference in wound infections or hematoma/seroma formation. Length of hospital stay and time to tolerate full feeds were very similar.

A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 490 infants randomized to single incision or conventional laparaoscopic pyloromyotomy. The two approaches were similar with regards to operative tmie, length of hospitalization, and complications.

A systematic review of 15 observational studies with 2964 patients found that while umbilical incision leaves a smaller scar than right upper quadrant incision, it is also associated with more complications.
Variations to allow easier access with the UMB approach include the squeeze technique and sliding umbilical window technique.
Outpatient pyloromyotomy via endoscopy has also been described, but long-term data are pending.
A formal training program was associated with a very low complication rate for the LAP technique in five surgeons.
A systematic review of 5 studies found no difference in the likelihood of surgical site infection with the use of prophylactic antibiotics.
Preoperative IV fluid therapy is needed to correct dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, and alkalosis.
Patients should not receive oral feedings prior to surgery.
Postoperative oral feedings ad lib result in more episodes of emesis, but shorter time to full feeds and shorter time to discharge compared with those whose feedings are held for more than 8 hours.

Anesthesia with remifentanil compared with halothane results in similar safety and recovery measures, except for greater incidence of postoperative new onset apnea following halothane-based anesthesia.
PS is currently managed in the hospital setting as patients require preoperative IV fluid, pyloromyotomy, and postoperative resumption of feedings, but outpatient treatment has been reported.
Pyloromyotomy complication rate is 2.71% and mortality rate is 0.1%. B
High-volume surgeons and hospitals have lower complication risk and lower cost compared with low-volume surgeons and hospitals. B
Ultrasound of pylorus muscle can be abnormal for up to 5 months postoperatively. B
